doc.title: Lorraine Feather interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, March 22, 2023

title: Dance, theater and Circle in the Square; parents' reaction
summary: Dance lessons at 12, a school production of Electra, a scholarship in New York and waitressing; her parents were upset about her moving.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: You moved to Los Angeles and then you returned to New York. Do you recall if your parents were supportive of your intentions for a career in music?

Well at the time I was trying to have a career in theater because I had — I started taking dance lessons when I was 12. My mom, I think she was under the impression that it was cotillion or something, that I was going to make friends and meet people. And it wasn’t like that. It was a jazz dance class led by this guy Carlton Johnson who is fantastic. He’s not with us anymore but they had a conga player for the exercises and then they would play Motown music and I got totally smitten and started taking class constantly. I really didn’t have the body for dance and I started too late. But then that shifted. I went to a Catholic girls’ school for just one year because my friend was going there, Jeri Southern’s daughter Kathryn King. And I didn’t particularly care for it, but they were doing an all-girl production of “Electra” the Greek tragedy. The lead got sick and I said, “I can do it” — sort of like saying I could write lyrics, “I think I could do it” because I was pretty good at, very good at memorizing mostly. And so I did it. I played the part and I can’t imagine that I was very good but my class all stood up at the end. And I’d been sort of shy and dorky and didn’t really consider myself a popular girl but it was exciting being on stage and being part of this story. So I thought well that’s what I’m going to do. I’m going to go to New York and be an actress. So I switched over to Hollywood High for the end of my high school career and I started doing after-school stuff and I won an © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

award for some little competition. And then at 18 — well actually 17, I got a little scholarship to study at Circle in the Square, a theater in New York. And then I stayed on when I was 18 and got a waitress job, my friend joined me and got a waitress job and I proceeded to waitress a lot and occasionally I would get into a show. But your original question was do you recall how your parents felt about it?

That was five minutes ago, I know. But yes, they were rather upset. They didn’t expect me to leave California like that and it was just upsetting to them that I was so far away and, you know, you’re going to be a cocktail waitress? You’re going to be dating musicians and running wild all over New York? All of which was true of course. And I did get in “Jesus Christ Superstar” at one point. I did it on the road and I did it on Broadway. I was in a tour, I was in the original theater thing, but mostly I just waitressed a lot, something that I was not good at particularly. When I was in my mid-20s I got a job singing back-up for Grand Funk Railroad.
